revisions.body: At the end of the craft analogy, Socrates puts two figures between a name and its correctness: the lawgiver makes the name, while the dialectician supervises the making. One way to read this is that “by nature” names are not simply whatever a maker happens to produce; natural fit becomes a standard that making must answer to and an expert must judge. Does that preserve Cratylus’s claim, or quietly make dialectical expertise the decisive test?

Before Homer enters, Socrates offers Hermogenes two routes to the correctness of names. The first runs through the sophists, including Protagoras, whose teaching Callias paid to receive. Hermogenes says he does not accept Protagoras’s truth at all, so he regards asking Callias to pass on that teaching as strange. Socrates then redirects him to Homer and the other poets. The poetic route is introduced as an alternative after Hermogenes’ objection, not as the only source of authority.

To choose between the boy’s two names, Socrates constructs a chain rather than quoting a ready-made Homeric verdict. Hermogenes assents that wiser people name more correctly and that men, as a class, are wiser than women. Socrates then brings in Homer’s report of the two names and treats Astyanax as the preferred one. Homer supplies the naming material; Socrates supplies the inferential bridge that turns it into a conclusion about correctness.

Socrates’ safeguard has a double effect. It presents the inquiry as modest and pious, but it also gives him room to speculate boldly about what human namers may have thought. My reading is that the disclaimer is meant to remain unstable: humility protects the conversation from impiety while daring interpretation proceeds under its cover. Listen for that tension rather than deciding too quickly whether the hedge is sincere, strategic, or both.

The central reversal is that Hades’ power is recast as attraction rather than coercion. Socrates makes desire for becoming better the strongest bond, so remaining with Hades can be heard not as confinement imposed from outside but as attachment to improvement. That is an interpretive gamble, not a demonstrated psychology: the argument persuades by changing the question from “Why can’t the dead escape?” to “What could make them want to stay?”

Socrates does not make Artemis’s name yield a single answer. He places several routes beside one another—soundness and order, virginity, knowledge of virtue, and hostility to sowing—and then leaves open whether the namer used one or all. That is the useful pressure point: the list behaves less like a verdict than a demonstration of how easily an etymology can multiply its grounds.

The justice etymology turns into a report about inquiry under pressure. Socrates says his questioning begins from secret instruction, but asking what justice is produces a series of competing reported answers: sun, fire, the heat in fire, and finally an unnamed speaker’s appeal to what Anaxagoras says justice is—mind. The sequence does not establish any answer; it leaves Socrates in greater aporia. The dramatic point is the gap between explaining a name and knowing what the just is.

revisions.title: From exact likeness to mixed correctness
revisions.body: Socrates loosens Cratylus’s demand for exact likeness: a perfect copy would be a second thing, not an image. The example of skleros then presses the point, since an unfitting letter can still signify through custom. Together these moves shift the issue from likeness alone to a mixed account of how names work.

The concession here is not a reversal. Socrates retains likeness as the preferred measure: names are best when as many letters as possible fit their things. But he also says convention is necessary for correctness, because likeness’s pull is insufficient by itself. The point is to separate an ideal of fittingness from the conditions that make naming work.
